name: Vitamin A (retinyl palmitate) from liver

lead: Animal liver and some supplements supply preformed vitamin A (retinol and retinyl esters), and people eat liver hoping for clearer, healthier-looking skin.

Vitamin A is the nutrient the body uses for skin cell turnover, which is why retinoids are so established in skincare. Retinyl esters are the storage form held mostly in liver; once absorbed they supply retinol for vision, skin and growth. Trials of dietary liver for appearance have not been run.

paras: People eat liver as a food a few times a week, or take liver-derived products such as desiccated liver capsules, usually as part of a broader nose-to-tail or nutrient-dense diet. Any skin change users report tends to be described over weeks to months.

Too much preformed vitamin A causes hypervitaminosis A, with nausea, headache, vision changes, skin peeling, hair loss, bone pain and liver damage. The US Institute of Medicine upper intake is 3,000 micrograms per day for adults and lower for children. Pregnancy and liver disease call for close monitoring of intake.

angle.text: Diet communities eat liver or take liver-derived products as a source of preformed vitamin A, aiming for clearer, healthier-looking skin. Vitamin A drives skin cell turnover, which is the basis of retinoid skincare; dietary liver has not been trialled for appearance.

lead: Preformed vitamin A, which includes retinol and retinyl esters such as retinyl palmitate, occurs in animal liver and in some supplements. Some diet communities eat liver or take liver-derived products for skin, vision and general nutrition. Hypervitaminosis A is the toxicity caused by excess preformed vitamin A, and Wikipedia lists liver, supplements and prescription medicines as the usual sources.[1]

Reported effects of excess intake include nausea, headache, vision changes, skin peeling and dryness, hair loss, bone pain and liver damage, and the condition is most strongly recognised with acute ingestion of very vitamin A-rich livers such as polar bear liver.[1] The US Institute of Medicine tolerable upper intake for adults is 3,000 micrograms per day.[1]
infobox: Animal liver, fish liver oils, supplements

paras: Retinyl esters are the storage form of vitamin A in animals, and about 80 to 90% of body reserves are held in the liver.[1] Between 70 and 90% of preformed vitamin A is absorbed.[1] Provitamin carotenoids such as beta-carotene differ: Wikipedia states excess carotenoid intake causes only a harmless reversible orange skin tint, carotenosis.[1]

Wikipedia lists early symptoms of hypervitaminosis A as nausea, vomiting, dizziness, headache, drowsiness, irritability and visual changes. Other signs include dry skin and mouth, cracked lips, hair loss, increased sun sensitivity, bone pain, high blood calcium, raised intracranial pressure and liver damage.[1] Skin effects can include peeling, itching, dryness and yellowing.[1]

Tolerance varies genetically and children are described as especially sensitive.[1] US Institute of Medicine upper levels are 600 micrograms per day for ages 0 to 3, 900 for ages 4 to 8, and 3,000 for adults.[1] Pregnancy, liver disease, heavy alcohol use and smoking are listed among situations that warrant close monitoring of vitamin A intake.[1] Stopping intake is the standard treatment and most people fully recover.[1]

Wikipedia reports that polar bear, bearded seal and walrus liver are especially toxic, that the Inuit have traditionally avoided polar bear and bearded seal liver, and that in 1597 Gerrit de Veer and his crew became severely ill after eating polar bear liver on Novaya Zemlya.[1] The 1913 death of Xavier Mertz on Douglas Mawson's expedition has been attributed by some accounts to sled-dog liver, while another study ascribes it more to exhaustion and diet change.[1]

No studies found testing liver-derived vitamin A for appearance outcomes. Two registered trials in the clinical trial registry concern broader topics: a micronutrient supplementation study on children's growth and a vitamin D study in COVID-19; neither tests liver or retinyl palmitate for appearance.[2][3]
